observations.source_title: Obesitas pada Remaja dan Cara Mencegahnya
observations.observation: The plan places “Makan Siang” between morning and afternoon snacks and gives a rice, protein, and vegetable meal.
observations.limitations: The page does not state a clock time for lunch.

observations.source_title: Obesitas pada Remaja dan Cara Mencegahnya
observations.observation: The article uses “Makan Siang” as an unmarked meal heading alongside “Sarapan” and “Makan Malam.”
observations.limitations: One institutional example supports natural use but cannot measure everyday frequency.

observations.source_title: PRPM entry for tengah hari
observations.observation: The entry translates “lunch” in the midday-meal sense as “makan tengah hari.”
observations.limitations: A translation entry does not establish conversational preference.

observations.source_title: Dietetik & Sajian
observations.publisher: Hospital Kuala Lumpur, Kementerian Kesihatan Malaysia
observations.observation: The patient meal schedule labels its 12:00–1:00 pm meal “Makan Tengah Hari,” between breakfast and afternoon refreshments.
observations.limitations: Institutional menu wording does not quantify everyday speech.

observations.source_group: Kemkes obesity article 4259 + Hospital Kuala Lumpur meal schedule
observations.source_title: Paired Indonesian meal plan and Malaysian hospital schedule
observations.publisher: Kementerian Kesehatan Republik Indonesia; Hospital Kuala Lumpur
observations.observation: Both sources use the respective expressions as ordinary labels for the meal between breakfast and later meals.
observations.limitations: The comparison is based on two institutional contexts, not a balanced usage corpus.

observations.source_title: Masalah Gizi pada Lansia dan Cara Mengatasinya
observations.observation: Advice about eating says people who struggle to use “sendok dan garpu” can have their hands guided toward the mouth.
observations.limitations: The passage identifies an eating utensil but does not describe its shape.

observations.source_title: Masalah Gizi pada Lansia dan Cara Mengatasinya
observations.observation: The guidance uses “sendok dan garpu” without explanation for utensils used to eat.
observations.limitations: One edited source does not establish relative frequency against alternatives.

observations.source_title: Mediakom, edition 161
observations.observation: The recipe repeatedly uses “sendok makan” and “sendok teh” as ingredient measures.
observations.limitations: The cited lead concerns measuring spoons, so it does not by itself establish the preferred name of an eating spoon.

observations.source_title: PRPM entry for sudu
observations.observation: Kamus Pelajar defines the utensil sense as a small tool used to scoop food and gives “camca” as a synonym.
observations.limitations: The entry also lists unrelated senses; it does not rank “sudu” against “camca.”

observations.source_title: Adakah Kita Digalakkan untuk Menjilat Baki Makanan yang Melekat pada Sudu Selepas Makan?
observations.observation: The article uses “sudu dan garpu” for modern utensils used to bring food to the mouth.
observations.limitations: This is natural public usage, but no frequency comparison with “camca” was made.

observations.source_group: Kemkes elder nutrition article 1226 + Federal Territories Mufti article 442
observations.source_title: Paired eating-utensil usage
observations.publisher: Kementerian Kesehatan Republik Indonesia; Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan
observations.observation: The Indonesian source uses “sendok” and the Malaysian source “sudu” in parallel eating-with-fork contexts.
observations.limitations: The examples establish natural choices in these contexts, not population-wide frequencies.

access_failures.outcome: Internal error; no dictionary content was inspected.

observations.source_title: Isi Piringku: Pedoman Makan Kekinian Orang Indonesia
observations.observation: The guidance says one “piring” at each meal is filled with vegetables, fruit, staple food, and side dishes.
observations.limitations: The article does not give a formal physical definition of the dish.

observations.source_title: Isi Piringku: Pedoman Makan Kekinian Orang Indonesia
observations.observation: The national nutrition campaign uses “piring” in its title and repeatedly for an ordinary meal plate.
observations.limitations: A campaign's wording supports a neutral choice but does not provide corpus frequencies.

observations.source_title: PRPM entry for pinggan
observations.observation: The dictionaries define “pinggan” as a flat food vessel and explicitly give “pinggan makan” for a main-meal plate.
observations.limitations: A dictionary definition alone does not establish current preference.

observations.source_title: Adakah Kita Digalakkan untuk Menjilat Baki Makanan yang Melekat pada Sudu Selepas Makan?
observations.observation: The article calls the vessel holding a meal “pinggan” throughout its explanation.
observations.limitations: It is one institutional example; the DBP distinction between “pinggan” and smaller “piring” helps delimit the sense but does not measure usage.

observations.source_title: PRPM entries for pinggan and piring
observations.observation: DBP describes “pinggan” as the larger vessel used for rice or a main meal and Malaysian “piring” as a smaller dish for cakes or under a cup.
observations.limitations: This is a sense distinction, not direct evidence of conversational frequency; the separate contextual observation supplies usage.

observations.source_group: Kemkes Isi Piringku article + Federal Territories Mufti article 442
observations.source_title: Paired meal-plate usage
observations.publisher: Kementerian Kesehatan Republik Indonesia; Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan
observations.observation: An Indonesian meal guide uses “piring”; a Malaysian discussion of the vessel holding a meal uses “pinggan.”
observations.limitations: The comparison does not imply that either word is absent from the other variety.

access_failures.outcome: Internal error; no KBBI definition was inspected.

observations.source_title: Sokongan Minim APBD Bukan Masalah, Bupati Sugiri Jamin Kualitas Grebeg Suro Tetap Terjaga
observations.observation: A comparison involving a chef describes appealing food as “makanan enak.”
observations.limitations: The sentence is metaphorical, although “makanan enak” plainly concerns food quality.

observations.source_title: Ciri-ciri DM yang Sudah Parah
observations.observation: The article contrasts food that “rasanya enak” or “makanan enak” with healthy food, using “enak” without explanation.
observations.limitations: Natural use is visible; relative frequency against “sedap” was not measured.

observations.source_title: PRPM entry for sedap
observations.observation: The entries define a taste sense equivalent to “enak” and illustrate it with “kuih.”
observations.limitations: The entry also records smell and non-food senses.

observations.source_title: Makanan & Minuman
observations.observation: The page headlines its food selection “Makanan yang sedap.”
observations.limitations: The same page also calls food and dishes “enak” at lines 53 and 65–67, so it does not establish that “sedap” is the sole or invariably preferred choice.

observations.source_title: Makanan & Minuman
observations.observation: The same Malaysian food page uses “enak” for dishes and local food.
observations.limitations: This confirms a live alternative but does not quantify whether it is as common as “sedap.”

observations.source_group: Kemkes diabetes article 1852 + Penang Hill food page
observations.source_title: Paired food-description usage
observations.publisher: Kementerian Kesehatan Republik Indonesia; Penang Hill Corporation
observations.observation: Indonesian public guidance naturally uses “enak” for food taste; a Malaysian food page uses “sedap” prominently, while also using “enak.”
observations.limitations: The observations support natural choices, but “normal” as a frequency ranking remains unmeasured.

access_failures.outcome: Page inaccessible through the retrieval tool; no KBBI content was inspected.

observations.source_title: Kenali Anak dengan Sindroma Nefrotik dan Diet Sehatnya
observations.observation: The article names “saus keju,” “saus tomat,” “saus sambal,” and sauces served with siomay, bakso, and noodles.
observations.limitations: The examples establish food-sauce uses but do not define the full consistency range.

observations.source_title: Kenali Anak dengan Sindroma Nefrotik dan Diet Sehatnya
observations.observation: The article uses both generic “saus” and specific expressions such as “saus tomat” and “saus kacang.”
observations.limitations: It supports natural generic and specific use, not a measured claim of nationwide normality; “sambal” and “kecap” also name particular condiments.

observations.source_title: KBLI | SPPIRT
observations.publisher: Badan Pengawas Obat dan Makanan Republik Indonesia
observations.observation: Food categories include “saus cabe,” “saus tomat,” “saus tiram,” and other named sauces, alongside “sambal.”
observations.limitations: A regulatory product list is not evidence of conversational frequency.

observations.source_title: PRPM entry for sos
observations.observation: The food sense defines “sos” as a liquid or thick substance used to enhance food's flavour.
observations.limitations: The page also has an unrelated uppercase SOS entry; the dictionary alone does not establish preference.

observations.source_title: Panduan Mengatasi Masalah Pemakanan Kesan Dari Rawatan Kanser
observations.publisher: Institut Kanser Negara, Kementerian Kesihatan Malaysia
observations.observation: Food advice says to flavour meat, fish, and chicken with lime juice, spices, “sos,” and natural seasonings.
observations.limitations: This is a generic use in one institutional publication, not a frequency comparison.

observations.source_title: Chilli sauce, bottle (Sos cili dalam botol)
observations.publisher: Malaysian Food Composition Database Programme, Institute for Medical Research
observations.observation: The database labels bottled chilli sauce “Sos cili dalam botol.”
observations.limitations: This is a named product, and the database is associated with 1997; the generic contemporary use is better shown by the separate nutrition guidance.

observations.source_group: Kemkes nephrotic syndrome article 409 + National Cancer Institute nutrition guidance
observations.source_title: Paired food-sauce usage
observations.publisher: Kementerian Kesehatan Republik Indonesia; Institut Kanser Negara
observations.observation: The Indonesian article uses “saus” for food sauces; the Malaysian food advice uses generic “sos” among flavouring ingredients.
observations.limitations: Similar form and function are supported; relative everyday frequency was not tested.

observations.observation: The press release uses “biskuit” as an unglossed, familiar packaged-food category.
observations.limitations: The source supports a normal choice but does not compare it with alternative everyday terms.

observations.observation: The dictionaries define “biskut” as a dry baked snack, usually flat, thin, and crisp.

observations.observation: Patient advice offers “biskut” as an ordinary snack and later as an easily digested dry food.
observations.limitations: The page does not provide a date or a frequency comparison with other terms.

observations.limitations: The sources establish parallel natural use, not a measured frequency ranking.
